title: Implicit differentiation
examples: How do I remember to differentiate the y terms?
What if the equation has x squared and y squared?
Can you show me an example where I need to find the gradient at a specific point?

explain.say: Today we learn implicit differentiation to find slopes. We use this when y is not easily isolated. Think of equations like x squared plus y squared equals 25.

items: Find slopes when y is not isolated

explain.say: When we differentiate with respect to x, remember to use the chain rule for y. You must multiply by dy/dx every time you differentiate a y term. For example, the derivative of y squared is two y times dy/dx.

items: Use chain rule for y terms
Multiply by dy/dx for y terms

explain.say: Let us find the derivative of x squared plus y squared equals 25. Differentiating gives two x plus two y dy/dx equals zero. Now we solve for dy/dx to find the general slope.

To find the gradient at a point like one, two, we substitute the coordinates into our solved derivative. For x equals one and y equals two, the slope is negative three divided by two. So the gradient is negative three divided by two.

faq.q: What if I have a term like y cubed?
faq.a: You treat it just like y squared. You use the power rule and multiply by dy/dx. The derivative of y cubed is three y squared times dy/dx.
asks: How do I differentiate y to the power of three?
What is the derivative of y³?

faq.q: Do I need to solve for y first?
faq.a: No, that is the whole point of implicit differentiation. You keep y as a variable and differentiate term by term. You only solve for dy/dx at the very end.
asks: Must I make y by itself?
Can I leave y in the equation?

faq.q: What is the process for finding the gradient at a point?
faq.a: First, differentiate the entire equation with respect to x, remembering the chain rule for y terms. Second, solve the resulting equation for dy/dx. Third, substitute the given x and y values into the final expression for dy/dx.
asks: How do I use the point (1, 2) to find the slope?
What are the steps for finding the gradient?

faq.q: Does the derivative change if I use different variables?
faq.a: The process remains the same regardless of the variables used. You always differentiate with respect to the variable you are given, which is usually x. Always remember to multiply by dy/dx when differentiating y terms.
asks: Does it matter if I differentiate with respect to y?
Is the rule different for different variables?

faq.q: What if the equation is very complicated?
faq.a: Break it down into smaller parts. Differentiate each term separately, applying the product rule or quotient rule if necessary. Remember the chain rule for every y term.
asks: What if I have x times y?
How do I handle complex terms?

facts: Implicit differentiation is used when y cannot be easily written as a single function of x.
When differentiating a term involving y, you must multiply the result by dy/dx.
The derivative dy/dx represents the slope of the tangent line at a point.
The chain rule is fundamental to this differentiation technique.

quiz.say: If x squared plus y squared equals 1, what is the derivative dy/dx?
quiz.why: When you differentiate x squared plus y squared equals one, you get two x plus two y dy/dx equals zero. Solving for dy/dx gives the correct answer.

wrong.1: This mistake forgets to differentiate the y squared term correctly.
wrong.2: This mistake incorrectly assumes that the derivative of y squared is just y.
wrong.3: This mistake forgets to solve the equation for dy/dx.

quiz.say: Find the slope of the curve x times y equals 10 when x is three.
quiz.why: Differentiating x times y equals ten gives one times y plus x times dy/dx equals zero. Solving for dy/dx gives the correct slope formula.

wrong.1: This mistake forgets to differentiate the x times y term using the product rule.
wrong.2: This mistake finds the value of y, not the derivative.
wrong.3: This mistake incorrectly differentiates the product x times y.

quiz.say: What is the gradient at the point (2, 1) on the curve x squared plus y squared equals 9?
quiz.why: Using the general derivative dy/dx equals negative x divided by y, we substitute two for x and one for y to get the correct gradient.

wrong.0: This mistake forgets the negative sign from the differentiation process.
wrong.1: This mistake adds the coordinates instead of using the derivative formula.
wrong.2: This mistake incorrectly assumes the slope is zero at that point.
